questions.stem: The converse of the implication "if P, then Q" is:
options: if not P, then not Q
if not Q, then not P
questions.explanation: The converse swaps the hypothesis and conclusion. "If not Q, then not P" is the contrapositive, which is a different statement.

questions.stem: The contrapositive of the implication "if P, then Q" is:
options: if not P, then not Q
if not Q, then not P
questions.explanation: The contrapositive swaps and negates both parts. "If not P, then not Q" negates without swapping; it is the inverse and is not equivalent to the original.

questions.stem: An implication and its contrapositive:
options: have truth values with no fixed relationship
are always both true or both false
are both true only when the converse is true
questions.explanation: An implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, which is why proving the contrapositive proves the original. The converse can differ in truth value.

questions.stem: Consider the true statement "if an integer is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3". Its converse is:
options: true, because 6 is a multiple of 3
true, because it is the contrapositive
questions.explanation: The converse is "if an integer is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 6", and 9 is divisible by 3 but not by 6. The number 12 is divisible by both, so it does not disprove anything.

questions.stem: The contrapositive of "if an integer is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 3" is:
options: if an integer is not divisible by 3, then it is not divisible by 6
if an integer is divisible by 3, then it is divisible by 6
if an integer is not divisible by 6, then it is not divisible by 3
an integer is divisible by 6 and not divisible by 3
questions.explanation: Swap and negate both parts: not divisible by 3 implies not divisible by 6, which is true. The third option negates without swapping and is false, for example for 9.

questions.stem: In logic, P ⇔ Q means that:
options: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P are both true
P ⇒ Q is true but Q ⇒ P may be false
P and Q are both true statements
P and Q cannot both be true
questions.explanation: Equivalence (if and only if) means each statement implies the other. P ⇒ Q alone is a one-way implication.

questions.stem: For an integer n, which of these is a true equivalence?
options: n is prime ⇔ n is odd
n is even ⇔ n² is even
questions.explanation: An even n has an even square, and an odd n has an odd square, so both directions hold. The others fail one way: n = −2 has n² = 4 and n² > 1, and 2 is prime but even.

questions.stem: Which use of the implication symbol is correct for real x?
questions.explanation: If x = 3 then certainly x² = 9. The reverse fails because x = −3 also gives x² = 9, and x = −4 satisfies x² > 9 without x > 3.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly uses the equivalence symbol for real x?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 3 and adding 3 are reversible, so x + 3 = 5 and x = 2 imply each other. In each of the others, one direction fails, for example x = −2 satisfies x² = 4.

questions.stem: In mathematical statements, the symbols ∀ and ∃ mean:
options: "is an element of" and "is not an element of"
questions.explanation: ∀ is the universal quantifier, "for all", and ∃ is the existential quantifier, "there exists". The symbol ∈ means "is an element of".

questions.stem: The negation of "all of the swans on the lake are white" is:
options: some swans on the lake are white
at least one swan on the lake is not white
no swan on the lake is white
every one of the swans on the lake is black
questions.explanation: To deny that every swan is white, one non-white swan is enough. "No swan is white" claims far more than the negation needs.

questions.stem: The negation of "∀x ∈ ℝ, x² ≥ 0" is:
questions.explanation: Negating "for all" gives "there exists", and the negation of x² ≥ 0 is x² < 0. Keeping ∀ gives a much stronger claim than the negation.

questions.stem: The negation of "there exists an integer n such that n² = 2" is:
options: there is no integer n such that n² ≠ 2
there exists an integer n such that n² ≠ 2
questions.explanation: Negating "there exists" gives "for all", with the condition negated. "There exists n with n² ≠ 2" is true but is not the negation; both it and the original could be true together.

questions.stem: The negation of "if it rains, then the match is cancelled" is:
options: it does not rain and the match is cancelled
it rains and the match is not cancelled
if it does not rain, then the match is not cancelled
if it rains, then the match is not cancelled
questions.explanation: The implication is false only when the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails, so its negation is "rain and not cancelled". The negation of an implication is not another implication.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is true?
questions.explanation: Every real square is non-negative. The second fails at x = 0, the third has no real solution, and the fourth fails at n = 0 and n = 1.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is correct?
questions.explanation: √2 is irrational, so it belongs to ℚ′, the irrational numbers. It is real but not rational, so it is not in ℚ or ℤ.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is FALSE?
questions.explanation: ℤ⁺ is the positive integers 1, 2, 3, ..., and 0 is neither positive nor negative. −3 is an integer, 0.75 = 3/4 is rational and π is real.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational?
questions.explanation: √8 = 2√2, which is irrational. √(16/9) = 4/3, the recurring decimal equals 3/11 and 22/7 is a fraction, so all three are rational.

questions.stem: Which fraction has a terminating decimal expansion?
questions.explanation: In lowest terms, a fraction terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5; 40 = 2³ × 5, and 7/40 = 0.175. The denominators 3, 12 and 7 contain other primes.

questions.stem: As a fraction in lowest terms, 0.444... (4 repeating) equals:
questions.explanation: Let x = 0.444...; then 10x = 4.444..., so 9x = 4 and x = 4/9. The value 4/10 = 0.4 terminates, so it is not equal to the recurring decimal.

questions.stem: As a fraction in lowest terms, 0.272727... (27 repeating) equals:
questions.explanation: Let x = 0.2727...; then 100x = 27.2727..., so 99x = 27 and x = 27/99 = 3/11. Multiplying by 10 instead of 100 does not line up the repeating blocks.

questions.stem: As a fraction in lowest terms, 0.1666... (only the 6 repeating) equals:
questions.explanation: Let x = 0.1666...; then 100x = 16.666... and 10x = 1.666..., so 90x = 15 and x = 15/90 = 1/6. Treating 16 as the repeating block gives 16/99.

questions.stem: As a fraction, 1.2353535... (with only 35 repeating) equals:
questions.explanation: Let x = 1.23535...; then 1000x = 1235.3535... and 10x = 12.3535..., so 990x = 1223 and x = 1223/990. Using 999 assumes all three decimal digits repeat.

questions.stem: A counterexample to a general statement is:
options: a proof that the converse of the statement is true
a list of many cases that support the statement
a single case for which the statement is false
a case for which the statement is true
questions.explanation: One case where the statement fails is enough to show that a "for all" statement is false. Any number of cases that support it can never prove it.

questions.stem: Which value of x is a counterexample to "for all real x, x² > x"?
questions.explanation: At x = 1/2, x² = 1/4, which is less than 1/2, so the statement fails. At x = −1, x² = 1 > −1, so the statement holds there.

questions.stem: Which value of n is a counterexample to "n² + n + 41 is prime for every positive integer n"?
questions.explanation: At n = 40, n² + n + 41 = 1681 = 41², which is not prime. The values at n = 1, 10 and 39 are 43, 151 and 1601, all prime.

questions.stem: Which pair is a counterexample to "for all real a and b, if a² = b², then a = b"?
questions.explanation: For a = 2 and b = −2, a² = b² = 4 but a ≠ b. The pair 3 and 9 does not satisfy the hypothesis a² = b², so it cannot be a counterexample.

questions.stem: In a proof about integers, an arbitrary odd integer is best written as:
questions.explanation: Every odd integer is one more than an even integer 2k, so 2k + 1 with k an integer covers them all. Particular examples such as 3, 5 and 7 cannot prove a general result.

questions.stem: To prove that the sum of two odd integers is even, write them as 2a + 1 and 2b + 1. Their sum is:
questions.explanation: (2a + 1) + (2b + 1) = 2a + 2b + 2 = 2(a + b + 1), a multiple of 2. Dropping the two 1s gives 2a + 2b, which is an arithmetic error even though it is also even.

questions.stem: To prove that the product of two consecutive odd numbers is odd, write them as 2k − 1 and 2k + 1. Their product is:
questions.explanation: (2k − 1)(2k + 1) = 4k² − 1, a difference of squares, and 4k² − 1 = 2(2k² − 1) + 1 has the form of an odd number. The middle terms cancel, so 4k² + 1 is a sign error.

questions.stem: In proving that 5n² + 3n + 6 is even for all n ∈ ℤ, one approach writes it as (4n² + 2n + 6) + (n² + n). The key step is that:
options: n² + n is even because n is always even
n² + n = n(n + 1) is a product of consecutive integers, so it is even
n² + n is even because n² is always even
5n² + 3n is always an odd number, so adding the even number 6 makes the total even
questions.explanation: One of n and n + 1 is even, so n(n + 1) is even, and 4n² + 2n + 6 = 2(2n² + n + 3) is even, so the sum is even. n² is odd when n is odd, so that claim is false.

questions.stem: To prove "for n ∈ ℤ, if n² is even then n is even" using the contrapositive, you would:
options: assume n² is odd and show that n is odd
assume n is odd and show that n² is odd
assume n² is even and show that n is even
assume n is even and show that n² is even
questions.explanation: The contrapositive is "if n is not even, then n² is not even", so assume n = 2k + 1 and show n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 is odd. Assuming n even proves the converse instead.

questions.stem: A proof by contradiction begins by:
options: checking the statement for several examples
assuming that the statement to be proved is false
assuming that the statement to be proved is true
proving the converse of the statement
questions.explanation: You assume the negation and deduce something impossible, so the negation must be false and the statement true. Assuming the statement itself would be circular.

questions.stem: In the proof that √2 is irrational, you assume √2 = a/b with a and b integers having no common factor, and show a² = 2b². The contradiction reached is that:
options: a must be odd while b is even
b must be zero, which is not allowed
a and b are both even, so they have a common factor 2
a must be odd, because a² = 2b² is twice a perfect square
questions.explanation: From a² = 2b², a² is even, so a is even; writing a = 2k gives b² = 2k², so b is even too. Then a and b share the factor 2, contradicting the assumption that a/b is in lowest terms; a is even, not odd.

questions.stem: In the proof that √3 is irrational, you assume √3 = a/b in lowest terms and reach a² = 3b². The next step is that:
options: 3 divides a², and since 3 is prime, 3 divides a
a² is even, so a is even
b² = 3a² follows, so b must also be a multiple of 3
a = 3b, so a is a multiple of b
questions.explanation: Since a² = 3b², 3 divides a², and because 3 is prime it must divide a. Writing a = 3k then gives b² = 3k², so 3 divides b as well, the contradiction. The equation is a² = 3b², not b² = 3a², and the parity argument used for √2 does not apply.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about real numbers is always true?
options: An irrational number times an irrational number is irrational
A rational number times an irrational number is irrational
A rational number plus an irrational number is irrational
An irrational number plus an irrational number is irrational
questions.explanation: If r + x = q with r and q rational, then x = q − r would be rational, a contradiction. The others have counterexamples: √2 + (−√2) = 0, √2 × √2 = 2 and 0 × √2 = 0.

questions.stem: To prove by contradiction that no integers m and n satisfy 6m + 3n = 1, you assume such integers exist. The contradiction is that:
options: m and n would both have to be negative
the left side is always an even number, but 1 is odd
m would have to equal n
the left side is a multiple of 3, but 1 is not
questions.explanation: 6m + 3n = 3(2m + n), a multiple of 3 for any integers m and n, but 1 is not a multiple of 3. The left side is not always even: m = 0 and n = 1 give 3.
